messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Parata is a 63-year-old Māori man, married and working as a senior financial analyst at a mid-sized investment firm in Auckland's financial district. He was referred for psychological assessment following a significant deterioration in his functioning over the past eighteen months, tracing back to the night his car was struck by a freight truck on a rural highway outside the city.

It had been a late evening in winter. Rangi had been driving home from a client dinner, the road dark and largely empty. A truck, whose driver had fallen asleep at the wheel, crossed the centre line and hit Rangi's vehicle almost head-on at speed. The impact was catastrophic. His car was spun off the road and came to rest in a drainage ditch, partially submerged. For what felt to Rangi like an eternity — later confirmed to have been over forty minutes — he was trapped in the wreckage in near-total darkness, the engine ticking and groaning around him, the smell of petrol and hot metal filling the cabin. He could hear other vehicles passing on the road above, their engines and tyres audible but their headlights unable to find him in the ditch. He was certain, at several points during those forty minutes, that he was going to die alone in the dark.

He survived with serious but ultimately treatable injuries. Physically, he recovered well. Psychologically, the months that followed told a different story. He returned to work after three months of medical leave, and it was there that the shape of his suffering began to reveal itself. The firm's underground car park, dimly lit at the far end near the stairwell, became something Rangi could not simply walk through. The moment he moved from the brightness of the street into that enclosed, shadowed space, his body would respond before he had formed any conscious thought — heart hammering, breath shortening, legs slowing. He had come to believe that his nervous system simply could not be trusted to wait for his mind to catch up, and this frightened him as much as the dark itself.

The smell of petrol, encountered at a service station or even near a colleague's car, could pull him back into the wreck without warning — not as a recollection he chose to visit, but as something immediate and present, the darkness and the smell and the sounds of the highway above him arriving all at once as though the accident were unfolding again in real time. He would sometimes hear, clearly and involuntarily, the grinding of metal and the distant passing of engines, as vivid as if he were still in the ditch. These moments were not, to Rangi, memories in any ordinary sense. They felt like the present tense.

He had stopped driving at night entirely. He had also, more gradually and more reluctantly, begun avoiding any situation that required him to be in a dark or enclosed space — underground venues, windowless meeting rooms, the cinema he and his wife had visited together regularly for years. His wife, Hinerangi, had at first been patient and accommodating, but the cumulative weight of his withdrawal had begun to strain their relationship. She had asked, carefully and with evident love, whether he was perhaps avoiding things that might actually help him heal. He had not been able to explain to her why thinking about the event felt, to him, like a risk he could not afford to take — that if he allowed himself to go there, he was certain he would not be able to hold himself together.

At work, Rangi had taken to sitting only in seats that faced the door and arriving early enough to identify every exit before colleagues filled the room. He woke most nights in the small hours, lying rigid in the dark beside his sleeping wife, listening and checking. He had come to believe that vigilance was not a burden but a necessity — that the world had revealed itself as a place where catastrophe could arrive without warning, and that the only rational response was to remain perpetually alert.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a morning when he sat in his car in the firm's car park for forty-five minutes, unable to make himself go in. He had sat there, a man of thirty years' professional experience, and wept. What he most hoped for, he said at intake, was to be able to sit in a dark room with his wife and watch a film again. What he most feared was that the person capable of doing that no longer existed.
